Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you for standing by. Welcome to the TFI International third quarter conference call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. Following the presentation, we will conduct a question-and-answer session. Callers will be limited to one question and a follow-up. Again, that's one question and a follow-up, so that we can get to as many callers as possible. Further instructions for entering the queue will be provided at that time. Please be advised that this conference call will contain statements that are forward-looking in nature and subject to a number of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. I would also like to remind everyone that this conference call is being recorded on Friday, October 30th, 2026. Joining us on today's call are Alain Bédard, Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer, and David Saperstein, Chief Financial Officer. I would now like to turn the call over to Alain Bédard. Please go ahead, sir.
Alain Bédard: Thank you very much, operator, and welcome everyone to this morning's call. Yesterday, after market close, TFI International reported another quarter of solid results with a standout performance from our truckload segment. Overall, adjusted diluted EPS was $1.67, up nearly 40% over the prior year's of $1.20. Our overall operating income grew 17% to $180 million, despite an office-related real estate impairment charge, and this was driven by truckload operating income that nearly doubled, and logistics operating income that was up almost 60%. Another important highlight is that this was the second consecutive quarter that TFI International achieved a sub-90% operating ratio on a consolidated basis. Of significant importance to our business strategy, we generated another $116 million of free cash flow, bringing our year-to-date total to more than $440 million, even while investing for growth. As a result, our leverage ratio further improved this quarter, as I'll discuss in a moment. This very solid financial foundation allows us to thoughtfully invest for the future during up and down cycles alike and also allows us to return excess capital to shareholders whenever possible, which we did both during and subsequent to the third quarter, as I'll also discuss. Taking a step back, our current strong performance is the direct result of the investment we made during the down cycle. We invested in our operation, we made strategic acquisitions, and as a result, we now have an enhanced focus on specialized freight, which improves diversification towards industrial end markets and across multiple modes of transportation. All the while, the talented men and women of TFI International have maintained their focus on efficiency and the related operating principle that drives our profitability. With that, let me quickly review our consolidated third quarter results before taking a closer look by business segment. Our top line total revenue before fuel surcharge of $1.9 billion was up 8% over the past year, while operating income reached $180 million, up 17%. Our operating margin of 9.7% was up 80 basis points over the prior year's quarter of 8.9%. Turning to our segment, we will begin with truckload, which simply had a phenomenal quarter and now represents 40% of segmented revenue before fuel surcharge at $753 million. That was up 10% the past year, and our revenue per truck per week, excluding fuel surcharge, climbed 13%. Operating income nearly doubled to $100 million, up from $53 million in a year-ago period, and our industry-leading adjusted OR of 86.7% marks a 560-basis-point improvement over the past year. Lastly, our return on invested capital for truckload was 8%, up from 6% last year. In addition to the tightening capacity industry-wide, these results directly reflects our favorable exposure to the right end markets, our emphasis on the specialized side of the business, and our limited capital intensity, with an optimal asset mix and improved fleet productivity. Next up is our LTL. LTL was 36% of segmented revenue before fuel surcharge at $678 million, which was roughly flat year-over-year. Our adjusted OR was 91.3%, and operating income was $44 million. Again, that's including a non-cash impairment and equates to a return on invested capital of 11.1%. Finish up the segment, logistics also had a strong quarter, with revenue before fuel surcharge of $437 million, up a robust 19% YoY, and logistics now accounts for 23% of our segmented total. Perhaps more impressive, our operating income jumped 59% to $49 million, and that equates to 11.3% margin, up nearly 3 full percentage points from the prior year's of 8.4%. Our logistics return on invested capital was 14.9%. Turning to our balance sheet, as I mentioned, $440 million of year-to-date free cash flow has further added to our overall strength, and we ended September with an adjusted funded debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 2.1x. Please note that this is an updated measure, which excludes the letter of credit and contingent consideration, which affected the previously communicated banking covenant ratio. I'll wrap up my prepared remarks this morning with our updated outlook, which include full quarter adjusted EPS of $1.30-$1.40, which at the high end would represent a 28% YoY increase. In addition, we continue to expect year-over-year adjusted operating ratio improvement of 400 basis points-500 basis points in the truckload segment, 100 basis points-200 basis points for our logistics, and a slight decline maybe of 100 basis points, up to 100 basis points for our LTL. And lastly, in terms of our outlook, we continue to expect net CapEx, excluding real estate, to be in the range of $225 million-$250 million, demonstrating improved capital efficiency. As always, our outlook ranges assume no significant change in the operating environment. With that, operator, David and I are ready to take question. If you could please open up the lines.
Operator: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, if you'd like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. If you'd like to withdraw your question, press star two. As a reminder, please limit yourself to one question and a follow-up. One moment, please, for your first question. Your first question comes from Ken Hoexter from Bank of America. Please go ahead.
Ken Hoexter: Hey, great, good morning. You know, you ran through.
Alain Bédard: Go ahead.
Ken Hoexter: Alain, thank you. You ran through truckload and logistics in, I guess, more detail than LTL. Maybe just take the opportunity to dig into LTL. Talk about your thoughts on the U.S. performance, maybe talk about fuel, the benefit, and then throw that into your fourth quarter outlook. How should we think about the improvement potential and going into fourth quarter and next year?
Alain Bédard: Yeah. A very good question, Ken. If you talk about Canadian LTL, I mean, fuel is some kind of a tailwind because of our density, right? Our density in Canada is second to none. But in the U.S., it is the opposite kind of thing, our density is so bad that when you have inflation like we went through in Q2 and in Q3 with fuel, that turns to be some kind of more of a negative because our density is not that good. Okay, we do about 20,000 shipments a day. We cover all of the U.S., and our density is not good. Now, as you know, we have been going through a very rough patch in our U.S. LTL for the year 2025, 2026. We are not very happy at all with the result that we have in 2026. And we are in for major improvement, I think, going into 2027 with improvement in the team and all of that. But that being said, we tried something, Ken. Tried to grow organically at TForce Freight, and the results, our timing was probably bad because we tried that in Q1 of 2026 when the weather was not helping us at all, okay? If you remember January, February, I mean, it was, like, difficult. Even Dallas was tough to deal with. And then, you go into Q2, we end up with something like 22,000 shipments a day, and our guys are not able to manage that. I mean, it's just, we are really sad about that that we have to say that, but those guys were not able to do that, and then we end up with inflation on the linehaul because at the same time that our guys cannot, our driver in our linehaul department cannot take this excess volume, we have to go on the spot market. And the spot market in Q2 and in Q3 for linehaul is just killing us, right? So, we have that negative affecting us, and at the same time, also, we have tried to grow in terms of volume, but we had to discount a little bit on the price. It is like a double whammy where you get less revenue per shipment, at the same time, you got more cost per shipment. So, this does not work, okay? This is why when you look at our Q3 numbers, we did fantastic everywhere except our U.S. LTL, which is like a broken story. I mean, it is like we keep repeating the same story time over time, and hopefully, with the improved teams that we have on board now, okay, under Kal's leadership, we could finally get this ball up and running. Now, I am sure you saw in our MD&A, okay, another little thorn in our shoe for our U.S. LTL is our six years partnership with our friend at UPS is coming to an end, okay, in early 2027, right? This is, again, another reason why, if you look at our forecast EPS for Q4, okay, because this partnership is ending early in 2027, we anticipate that some customers will have to find a solution somewhere, okay? We're working on a solution of our own, but this is difficult to do, to try to replace UPS with someone else, right? This is why we're very careful about the guidance that we're giving for Q4. We feel really good about our truckload, like I said on the script. We feel really good with our logistics, but another rock in our shoe on our U.S. LTL is what I just said about GFP, the partnership that we have for six years with UPS that will come to an end at the end of January 2027. Now, I mean, when you look at that, you say, "Hey, you've been at it for years and years and years," and I agree, and we were never able to turn the corner with this. I mean, 2021, 2022 were way better. 2023 was not so bad, but then 2024, 2025 with freight recession, increasing inflation on the cost, et cetera, et cetera. We believe that we're going to turn the corner in 2027. Now, that's an opportunity because if you look at our revenue, okay, and the small margin that we get out of that, I mean, once we fix that, I mean, TFI is going to be like, "Wow." That's the big rock that we have in our shoe, Ken, okay, but that's also the big opportunity down the road if we can fix that. And we have to fix it because, I mean, this is huge revenue for us, and the contribution is minimal, right? So, I mean, the good thing is we've acquired Daseke two years ago, and that Daseke ship has been turned around very, very fast. I mean, if you look at when we bought Daseke, these guys were running a 97%, 98% OR. In Q2, okay, we did a good job. In Q3, now we're coming with a sub-87% OR in our truckload compared to my best peers in the U.S. I mean, we're doing great. I mean, the Canadian operation is doing even better, okay, but our U.S. operation slowly is catching up, right?
Ken Hoexter: Yeah. Just to follow up, do you need to acquire to get the density there, or is that something you can do on your own?
Alain Bédard: It can. It's a union shop, right? The only other union shop, I mean, those guys, they do a great job. They're better than us, right? And for sure, I mean, we've tried to do something, and it never worked. So, the plan, Ken, has been simple, is that we're building, okay, in parallel to our 20,000 shipments, slowly we're going to start building in a non-union, okay, operation. Today, we do about 1,000 shipments a day, non-union, through Hercules, our U.S. operation. Hercules has got partnership with some of our Canadian business as well. But this is small, right? But, I mean, unless there's something upside that come to us, the plan is going to be really to slowly build that non-union, okay, like we do in Canada, because Ken, in Canada, we run both. We run union and non-union. So, to me, I mean, it's okay. We'll run a second network if we can. The idea is to bring more stability to our TForce Freight because, again, if you look at history, the way we used to do things in the U.S. is, okay, volume goes down, okay, because of December, January, we let go of people, then we call them back in March. Those guys are not available. You have to rehire. I mean, this is instability, and this is one thing that we're working on with Kal and his team, okay, to try to have a volume that is steady, okay, month-over-month, okay, in that 20,000 shipments a day range, which we are now.
Ken Hoexter: Right. Thanks for the thoughts, Alain. Appreciate it.
Alain Bédard: Very good, Ken.
Operator: Your next question comes from Scott Group from Wolfe Research. Please go ahead.
Scott Group: Hey, thanks. Good morning. Just a couple follow-ups on that LTL. Maybe, can you share where's the U.S. LTL margin right now? And the UPS relationship that's sort of ending, does this impact just the GFP business? Is that going away, or is there a broader impact than GFP?
Alain Bédard: No, Scott. The GFP thing is just that partnership that we have with UPS, okay? That's going to come to an end at the end of January 2027. After six years of partnership with UPS, as a reseller of UPS services, this is going to go away, okay? So, that's a GFP thing. About the profitability of our U.S. operation LTL, okay, for sure, when we reported 91% OR, okay, I mean, you can think that our U.S. operation is more closer to a 97% OR, and our Canadian operation is more like a sub-75% OR operation. But the size is not the same, right? We do about 10,000 shipments a day in Canada. We do 20,000 in the U.S.
Scott Group: Right. And then, so can you just, like, how big is this GFP business today?
David Saperstein: Well, the operating income in Q3 was a little over $4 million.
Scott Group: Okay. Thank you, David. And then, maybe just, like, Alain, bigger picture, like, in that first question, you said, "It feels broken. We have no density." But you also said like, "We think we can improve it in 2027." So, like, help us square those two comments. And then, like, when you think about, like, allocating capital to the business, it felt like a few years ago, we wanted to allocate more capital to LTL. We were thinking about.
Alain Bédard: Yes.
Scott Group: De-emphasizing truckload.
Alain Bédard: Yes.
Scott Group: Like, are we now, is the message different that we want to allocate more capital to truckload, or how should we think about where you want to, like, invest incremental capital?
Alain Bédard: Okay. You know what, Scott, that's a very good question. So, if you look at opportunities right now, okay, so in our U.S. truckload operation, or even our Canadian operation, I mean, we still have a good year to go to fine-tune everything that we do in our U.S. truckload operation. But let's say something nice comes around, okay, in mid-2027, for sure, we're in a position to look at it. On the LTL side, on the Canadian side, I mean, there's not much that we can do. But on the U.S. side, union side of our operation, I mean, there's nothing we can do except build some kind of a non-union network in parallel to the network that we have. In the meantime, okay, for sure, we're adapting the network, okay, to a 20,000-shipment company. As an example, we're going to have a transaction with one of our friends in Chicago, where they will take over one of our terminals. We're in discussion also with one of our terminals in the New York area to reduce our footprint, okay, to that 20,000, 22,000 shipments a day. And also, at the same time, our focus is going to be to try to bring more density to that 20,000 shipments. Try to, you know, the average mile that we drive today between each and every stop in our P&D is about twice as much as our Canadian operation. Why is that? Because in Canada, we focus on trying to do business with customers that are close by and not run 100 mi to do a delivery, right? This culture, we've been working at it with our friends there at the U.S. LTL, but it seems to be difficult to do. We're getting some support. We just hired an executive that hopefully is going to be able to help us drive change. But there are more team members that we need to add to drive more change and to bring that density down, because fuel is high, okay? In Canada, like I said, with Ken, it's a tailwind for us, okay? But in the U.S. truckload or in our U.S. LTL, it's not a tailwind. It's more of a headwind, right? Truckload has been, I mean, we did fantastic in Q3, even with that headwind in our truckload, but we did very poorly, okay, in our U.S. LTL in Q3 with that headwind, that cost inflation on our linehaul, because the market has been very hot, okay, on the spot. So, all of that really turned out to be not a great quarter for us at all. Now, in terms of investment, if you look at our CapEx, okay, this year, in our U.S. LTL, we did a lot of CapEx to support this company. I mean, we bought 1,500 trailers, okay, this year. We bought a little over 600 trucks. I mean, we continue to do the investment, okay, but the return has been not great at all, okay? So, this is why it's like, "Guys, we have to turn this thing around." I mean, there's no other solution. I'm very happy, like I said earlier, with the capital intensity of our truckload in the U.S., that it has improved tremendously. Our revenue per truck, okay, is up big time, not just because of the revenue per mile is up. The usage, the number of miles per truck is also up. We've also been able, with Steve and his team, to transform our U.S. truckload operation with more like niche carriers. If you just look at one of our carriers, SPD, on the West Coast, I mean, these guys, they were like jack of all trade, master of none. They were servicing the aerospace industry, like Boeing and Bombardier and others. That was with 75 trucks. But they had also another 125 trucks losing money. So, we said, "No, no, forget about that." Those 125 trucks have been moved to Wylie, and now, SPD is making money with the truck, making money with the brokerage. We've also attacked our friend in Texas, Lone Star. Again, very great carrier, okay, with the wind, with the data center and all of that. But they also had an over-the-road operation that was just killing them. So, we said, "No, no, this is over, my friend." This has just happened in Q3. Over the road is going to Wylie. Okay, fine. So, this is the fine-tuning that Steve and his team still have to do. We're working on COTC right now, and then it's South Shore. That's why I'm saying 2027, Q4, 2026, 2027 for our truckload, we see great improvement there. Truckload is great. Logistic is great. U.S. LTL is not. And that's, again, I mean, I feel like I'm a broken record on that. We got to correct the situation. We know what to do. It's just, we need the soldier, we need the management to jump in and do the right thing.
Scott Group: Thank you, Alain.
Alain Bédard: Okay.
Scott Group: Thank you very much. Appreciate it.
Alain Bédard: Pleasure.
Operator: Your next question comes from Jason Seidl from TD Cowen. Please go ahead.
Jose: Hi, morning. This is Jose on for Jason Seidl. Maybe, just to go back to the U.S. LTL, Alain, revenue per shipment, I think.
Alain Bédard: Yep.
Speaker 5: Decelerated a bit here in the third quarter.
Alain Bédard: Yep.
Speaker 5: Last quarter, you spoke about, you know, 3PL mix being a factor. I'm just wondering.
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
Speaker 5: If that's still a factor in the third quarter, and then, if that was the case, then thoughts on how you plan to rationalize that?
Alain Bédard: Yeah. It is still a factor in Q3, but over the course of Q3, it's been improving. So, Q3 is three months, right? So, it was not good in July at all. Okay, it got a little bit better in August and better in September, and we keep improving that for our Q4 situation there. So, yeah, it's been an ongoing thing where our commercial team has been really hard working at it. So, yeah.
Speaker 5: All right. Thanks. That's helpful. Then, maybe just sticking on the, you mentioned the linehaul pressures here. Can you maybe give us some detail, maybe remind us how much rail you utilize presently, and maybe on the trucking side, is there an opportunity to kind of enter more contract-type exposure and reduce spot?
Alain Bédard: Yeah. Yeah. So, if you look at our situation today, I mean, about 55% of our miles is done through our own people, okay, our own drivers. About 20-some percent is rail, okay? And then, we have about 125 owner op, okay, that is also exclusive to us. And over above that, we have also contract, but when the volume went from, let's say, 19,000 shipments to 22,000 at the peak, we had to go on the spot market because, I mean, we didn't have enough power with our own team. Okay. We move a little bit more volume on the rail, but there again, I mean, then you end up with service issue. It's not the solution. So, we went on the spot. The spot was about, what, $2.75, $2.90 a dollar, whereas, let's say, eight months ago, it was like $2.20, right? So, that killed us in Q2 and in Q3. Now, at the end of three, we're back to normal because now, okay, we don't have to go on the spot market to get power for our linehaul.
Speaker 5: All right. Very helpful. Thank you very much, Alain.
Alain Bédard: My pleasure.
Operator: Your next question comes from Ravi Shanker from Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.
Ravi Shanker: Great. Thanks, Alain, David. Thanks so much for the details so far. Alain, you have been very clear on the idiosyncratic changes you guys need to make in the LTL business. I would love to hear your characterization of the LTL market overall as well. Where do you see demand right now relative to where ISM is in the mid-50s? Where do you see the pricing environment? How do you see competition and capacity shaping up, et cetera?
Alain Bédard: Well, the chance we have in our U.S. LTL is our peers are smart. I mean, we are not competing with stupid peers. Our peers are really, really smart, doing a great job. So, this is why, to me, okay, volume is soft a bit. Yes, it has been soft for the last few years, but at least the pricing is holding. I mean, there is no, from what I can see, pricing war because we have smart leadership in the U.S. LTL, okay, with the leader running a 70% OR, with the second next one running an 80% OR. I mean, you got smart guys doing a great job on the market. So, to me, the market is soft a bit, but price-wise, I mean, us, we are the problem, us. I mean, it is not the market that is the problem, it is us, okay? So, we have to do a better job commercially to identify what fits, okay, and the average weight per shipment. You see another of our peers, weight per shipment is up. I mean, this is the way to go because you are paid by the pound, okay? So, I mean, our weight per shipment is down a bit, so that is the wrong direction, guys. So, we have to move this into more heavier industrial. We love us industrial freight. Why is that? Because this is us with our truckload operation. That is what we move. Everything is industrial. We do not move retail. We do not have, let us say, dollar store as a customer retail. We do not move that, us. We move industrial. So, again, those industrial customer have LTL. But us, with the old UPS approach, they were focused on retail freight. So, now, we are opening more doors with the size that we have now in truckload industrial freight, where we are saying to our U.S. LTL guys, "Guys, wake up," and let us piggyback our U.S. LTL commercial team working with our truckload commercial team to get more of that industrial freight in our LTL environment. At first, with the old team there, we got pushback. "Oh, there is lots of claim," blah, blah, all kinds of story. But now, this is something that is ongoing to try to improve the weight per shipment at the same time as the revenue per shipment. But Ravi, in my mind, this U.S. LTL market is way better than the Canadian one. It is way better. The leadership is great. The market is soft, but at least the pricing is holding, and the leaders are getting more dollars, right, per 100 weight. So, I mean, it's not the market, it's us.
Ravi Shanker: Understood. And maybe quickly as a follow-up on the TL side as well, shifting gears a little bit, can you talk about the potential upside you see for 2027, especially around rates and bid season, especially as 2027 kicks off?
Alain Bédard: Well, I think that on the truckload side, the market is still soft. I mean, the demand is not there. It's not really wow, but it's the supply, okay, because of the administration, okay, what these guys have been doing with CDL, illegals, the guy can't speak the language, and all that story, okay? So, this has helped us to a certain degree so far in 2026. But going into 2027, I think that this is some kind of a permanent change, and if the demand starts to grow, like in the building material, for example, I mean this is like dead for us. Who's buying a house now, right? Who's building? No one. Okay, interest rate's at 7%. Okay, fine. But this is going to come to an end at one point. So, building material is key to us, steel, aluminum, and all that. So, we feel very good about 2027 because at one point, the demand will start, the supply will stay constrained, and us, like I said, during the course of 2027, we still have some tweaks to do. Mr. Brookshaw and his team, they still have some improvement of our own to do, and it's going to take us another six months in 2027, maybe all year of 2027, to have a state-of-the-art U.S. operation like we have in Canada.
David Saperstein: Yeah, and the thing I'd add to that is the nature of our business, the structure of the business has changed, and you see that in the reduction in the capital intensity, right?
Alain Bédard: Oh, yeah.
David Saperstein: We have a principle, which is to do more with less, and you really see that here, right? You see more revenue with less trucks. As a result, the OR goes from 92% to 86.5% because depreciation expense is far lower, the productivity on the trucks is far higher. Our brokerage revenue in the quarter was up 49% YoY, right? So, we're basically taking our assets, we're putting them to the most productive use.
Alain Bédard: Right.
David Saperstein: Meaning, the end markets that are the most productive, the customers that provide the highest return for us, right, where we have real competitive advantage, niche businesses, and the rest we're brokering and we're using independent contractors. That's where our return on invested capital in truckload, it jumped from 6% to 8%. It's enormous. It's a 33% increase in ROIC year-over-year, and I would encourage you to benchmark other truckload players for true after-tax ROIC. Nobody's at 8%. Nobody's even close to 8%. The reason for that is that it's like a hybrid business. It's not a pure asset-based business. It's a hybrid business that we built in this way to get these returns, and you're seeing that transformation take place. When Mr. Bédard talks about these further adjustments that are still to come, in addition to the market, this is what we are talking about. We are talking about more right-sizing of the capital intensity and more increases in the returns as a result.
Alain Bédard: Yeah. And guys, on the brokerage, if I may add, I mean, we are not like some of our peers in the brokerage world, okay?
David Saperstein: No.
Alain Bédard: I mean, so us, we have specific carriers that we use, okay, all the time. I mean, we are not using Joe today and Peter tomorrow and then someone else the next day. No, no, no. Us, we have a portfolio of carriers that deal with us, okay, on a daily basis that we deal. The same is true of JHT, as an example, okay? When we are moving trucks for our OEMs, we have one of our agents that is going to do probably, out of the 250,000 trucks that we move, this guy will probably move for us 40,000 trucks, okay? So, it is brokerage for us, but we do not deal with 45 different companies. We deal with one guy, right, that we know that he has got coverage, that he has got insurance, right, that he is a professional, not an illegal guy that today decided to lease a truck and he becomes a truck driver.
Ravi Shanker: Understood. Thanks for both of the color.
Operator: Your next question comes from Walter Spracklin from RBC Capital Markets. Please go ahead.
Walter Spracklin: Yeah, thanks very much. Good morning, Alain. Good morning, David. Morning. Coming back to your costs, I have had a number of questions with regards to your cost structure perhaps being able, in theory, to be more insulated against some of the wage inflation aspects that other carriers might have that may be more reliant on owner-operators or may not be unionized, and therefore could see more competitive moves. We are not really seeing that in these results. Can you speak a little bit to, is that just kind of great in theory, but not in practice? Love to hear your thoughts on your cost structure there.
Alain Bédard: Yeah. So, Walter, I mean, are you talking about LTL or truckload or both?
Walter Spracklin: Mainly on the.
Alain Bédard: In general?
Walter Spracklin: Where you're seeing the most inflation. Yeah, in the areas where you're seeing the most labor inflation, wage inflation.
Alain Bédard: Oh, okay. On the truckload side, for sure, Walter, U.S. and on the Canadian side, I mean, as of Q2, we're starting to see, okay, some inflation on the salary, okay? I mean, that's a given. Why is that? Because there's the eternal shortage of drivers, right? If you would talk to Steve Brookshaw, he would tell you, "My main thing is I need drivers," right? So, what happens when you need drivers is the price or the cost of a driver goes up, right? So, we are going through some inflation for sure, okay, with the driver wage. But at the same time, we have to be more efficient with our asset, okay, our drivers and our trucks. So, this is what David was saying, okay, more revenue per trucks. Also, the other thing that Steve and his team has focused is the empty miles, right? Between, okay, the unloading of your customer and the reloading of your next customer, between the two, okay, nobody pays fuel surcharge. So, when you are buying fuel at $6/gal versus $3/gal a year ago, I mean, this is inflation to your cost, right? So, the smarter you are by improving your density in your truckload, that is going to be a huge benefit for you. So, that is the truckload. Now, on the LTL side, labor, okay, is not an issue so far because, like you said, in the U.S., most of our labor is unionized, so we have a contract, it is 3%, so we deal. It is the third party that we are using, okay, for linehaul or for the last mile. That is where we got a lot of cost increase, okay? This is why we had to go back to do it ourselves, okay, instead of using a third party that is going to cost $2.90/mi to haul a trailer from point A to point B, okay, whereas we used to pay on the spot or contract rate, $2.20. So, this is where we had inflation in Q3, and it will continue when you have inflation at 3%-4%. I mean, for sure, we are going to have cost pressure. So, this is why, like I said to Steve, we got to do more with less. So, forget about those guys that bring revenue of $3,000 a week on a truck. I mean, this guy, don't give him a truck. He is always sick, he is always on vacation, he this and that. No, no, forget about this guy. Okay, get this guy out. Okay, we need $5,000, $6,000 per truck per week, okay? Because under that, it is difficult to be profitable.
David Saperstein: Yeah, no. And as it relates to the LTL and the cost pressures we saw in the quarter, part of that was also related to the transition around the rate of volume growth. So, if you remember, last quarter, we had too much volume growth. The rate of growth was too high, so we raised price aggressively on the blanket 3PL rates to slow the rate of growth. And you see that, right? The year-over-year shipments in LTL is 4% this quarter as opposed to 7.5% last quarter. But those costs came out of the network over the course of the quarter, and not necessarily in lockstep with the volumes coming out. So, as we look, though, now towards the end of the quarter, the balance is there, and to October, the balance is there. And so, some of those excess cost lags were impacting Q3 and are no longer there today.
Alain Bédard: Yeah. Yeah. And you know what, Walter? When you think about the theory is, if a guy delivers 15 shipments a day, you give him two more, okay? This is going to be very profitable. But, if the guy comes back with those two shipments and you have to give that to a third party, I mean, it's a losing proposition, right? So, this also was part of our, you know, I was not very happy with what happened there, right? So, this is why I said, "Kal, we need stability. We need better management. We need to better manage our costs and manage our people." So, we have great terminals within the TForce Freight network, highly profitable terminal, but we also have dogs. So, we're attacking those dogs where you give a guy more shipment and you just come back with those shipment. He says, "Well, we'll do it tomorrow." No, no, because then, we miss service, my friend. You have to do it today. So, again, this is part of all this situation that we are aggressively working on. And that's also part of that inflation that we had to, because we had to hire a third party to do the delivery, okay, of that additional freight, if you want to call it that.
Walter Spracklin: That's great color. And Alain, I'm going to ask you a question. I don't know to what extent you're going to be able to answer it, but it is about kind of leadership succession plan. We just had a bunch of retirements in the railroad sector last night. Our friend [inaudible] announced he's putting up the gloves as well. When I look out to your plan and your strategy over the next year or two, you'd always articulated the idea of acquiring to build scale in LTL.
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
Walter Spracklin: And then spinning truckload and kind of going that path. If that gets delayed and we are not able to get the right acquisition and you are not able to bring in the right scale that you talked about and density that you are looking for, are you looking at any other avenues? Are divestitures in the works? Are there any other things that you are considering as we go toward a change in leadership eventually? We do not want you to retire, but when you do, I know it is inevitable, but how are you thinking about that over the next couple years if things do not pan out from an M&A perspective as you hoped in 2027 or 2028?
Alain Bédard: But you know what, Walter? We got a lot of opportunity on $150 million-$200 million EBITDA with low D&A, okay? We do not like D&A at all, okay? There is some that happened in Canada that we passed on, and my friend made the deal. Okay. Great. But we had to digest the Daseke acquisition. And if you go back, 2025 was not great for our truckload business. I mean, because we had all kinds of problems, okay, because of this acquisition that we were doing the integration. But if you look at 2026, forget about Q1, because Q1 was like the tail of 2025, but from Q2, we start to see the results of what Steve and his team have done in the U.S., and it is a confirmation in Q3. And we still have some work to do, but if the right thing, the right investment comes along, okay, sometimes in 2027, we are ready. Okay? We are ready. Now, it could be upsize. Okay. It could be a $100 million EBITDA company. It could be a $200 million-$300 million. I mean, we have got capital to justify through debt, $1 billion, $1.5 billion, okay, acquisition, cost of an acquisition. And what we look at is always the same thing, is the U.S. LTL, okay, we would like to do something there, okay, and the logistics. Us, we are a big fan of logistics, and I think that our team is doing it really, really well. I mean, just look at the results of Q3. I mean, those guys came in with an 11% bottom line. I mean, this is great news, and we are not stuck with all this issue of you are brokering to a jack-of-all-trade, and you got the risk, like some of our peers. Us, our logistic is not just brokerage. I mean, we do brokerage, yes, but we move trucks, we do all kinds of work for Ford, in contract logistics, et cetera, et cetera. So, it is not just one thing that we do, and we are really in control. So, if the right opportunity comes along with a great logistics company, that would be a fantastic fit. But we are not looking at a guy with a 2% bottom line. I mean, this is not for us. We leave that to the other guys.
Walter Spracklin: Appreciate the color as always, Alain. Thank you.
Alain Bédard: You're welcome.
Operator: Your next question comes from Brian Ossenbeck from JPMorgan. Please go ahead.
Brian Ossenbeck: Hey, good morning. Thanks for taking the question, guys. Just two quick follows. First on LTL, U.S. LTL. Is there any operational impact to the network when GFP doesn't get renewed? Does that affect density even further or, I guess, complexity of the network?
Alain Bédard: No.
Brian Ossenbeck: And then, just speaking of complexity, how would a non-union, I guess, bolt-on or expansion work functionally with the current footprint? Is that something you need to acquire more, need to expand, or maybe bifurcate how you use some of the terminals? Maybe just a little bit more detail on that, because it does sound like that's more part of the future plan here.
Alain Bédard: Okay. So, on that, Brian, GFP is like a brokerage operation for us. Okay? So, everything was done by UPS, our partner. Okay? So, it does not affect our operation at all. Okay? So, that's number one. Number two, what we're building as a non-union, okay, with just 1,000 shipments, it's more of an asset-light carrier, right? So, if you look at our capital intensity in Canada, I mean, it's really, really low. Why is that? Because we use a lot of third party, okay? The only thing really that we manage in Canada, except for TST where we have assets, okay, is the dock. And this is the direction that we're going in the U.S. in the non-union LTL operation, is that we're going to manage the dock, yes, us, but all the P&D, all the linehaul will be third party, right? So, why are we doing that? It's because we hate capital intensity. So, this is why we're going to start building that, because we believe that one day, okay, in the U.S., there will be an LTL company that's going to be an asset-light operation, like in the parcel world, right? So, you got this big blue machine that's running on third party everywhere, basically. Okay? So, if those guys decide one day to be in the LTL world, they will probably go asset-light. So, this is why us, we cannot be asset-light in our union environment, okay? We could do it to a certain degree, but not like 80%. So, like we did in Canada, okay, we are slowly going to build a non-union asset-light, okay, operation in the U.S. That's the goal. Unless we find a solid operator at a reasonable price, then we'll see. But in the meantime, if we got to go baby step trying to build this network, that is the intention. That's where we're going.
Brian Ossenbeck: Okay, understood. Thank you. Just for a quick follow-up, I guess it relates to that comment about going more asset-light. Looks like some of the reserves for accidents were up, and that includes a reversal, I guess, from the prior years. So, maybe you could just talk more broadly about the complications of going more asset-light in this sort of backdrop, and I guess how you're experiencing that right now, not only from a brokerage liability perspective, but also just from an auto liability claims and how that's also inflationary. Thanks.
David Saperstein: Yeah. So, our accident accrual this quarter was very much in line with normal, right? Most of that, a lot of it is in corporate costs, especially for the larger accruals, and you can see our corporate costs were around $14 million-$15 million, very normal for the quarter. What you saw last year this quarter was that we settled the claim for $5 million less than our accrual. That is a testament to the machine that we built to handle our accident liability. We've got a fantastic team that is out there settling claims early, sometimes on the spot. We're very, very close to this in the finance team, in terms of really following each of these cases, getting them done fast, making sure the accruals are right. So, really, the year-over-year change in the quarter should be viewed as a very positive thing. It's not an increase in accident expense. Yes, arithmetically, it's an increase, but really, what it is it's highlighting the fact that we got something done less than the cost of our accrual in the year prior. And more broadly, as it relates to managing this, the approach, of course, is to have kind of adequate risk management as it relates to the insurance program. But the most important thing to reduce accident claims is to reduce accidents. So, this is why we invest in technology. This is why we invest in driver safety. This is why we're very careful about all of these things. And when there are incidents, we deal with them aggressively and quickly and proactively, because time is against you in these things.
Alain Bédard: Yeah. And if I may add, in our truckload guys, we are starting to implement, okay, inward-facing camera. That's number one. We're also implementing, okay, to teach our driver simulator, okay, like, you know, those airline pilots, okay? So, we are introducing simulator, okay, to our JHT team, to our TForce Freight team, okay, so that you can test a driver, okay, in all kinds of different environment. Okay, so that's ongoing. Then, on top of that, if I go back to brokerage, pure brokerage that we do, okay, because our loss ratio is so minimal, okay, David, so what did we do with the insurance on that?
David Saperstein: Well, on the brokerage, we did go out and buy much higher limits, much higher coverage on the brokerage, and it cost us very little because our loss ratio in brokerage is zero.
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
Brian Ossenbeck: Okay. Very helpful. Thanks, guys.
Alain Bédard: You're welcome.
Operator: Your next question comes from Jordan Alliger from Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.
Jordan Alliger: Yeah. Hi, morning. Just a couple things. One, on the logistics front, which is doing quite well, is it primarily being driven by brokerage? I know you have other services in there as well. Can maybe talk a little bit about that? Then, secondly, just on the LTL, appreciate all the comments on it in terms of things to think about and how to fix. But Alain, do you have a timeframe for the fix where we could start to see better profitability? Is this six months, 12 months? And is there a point in time where you say, "Okay, we have to start the script over and come up with a new three-year plan?" Thanks.
Alain Bédard: Yeah. Okay. In terms of the time, we bought this company, think about that, five years ago, okay, in May of this year. It took us two years to get financial information that we can manage. Okay, so, 2021, 2022, all the way up to the summer of 2023. So, we've been at it for three years, and it's not doing well, right? So, we made some changes. We've invested in talent coming from outside the world, okay, the Canadian team, because what we've done since day one is we brought some Canadian guys to help the U.S. team. But now, okay, what we've been able to accomplish is to bring an executive from one of our peers that had retired, and we said, "Hey, maybe you're up to another challenge." I mean, so this guy joined us October 1st. So, I think that now, the recipe is to try to improve. I remember one of our shareholders, major shareholder, always told me, "Alain, you got to hire a super guy like one of your peers did." And us, we're saying, "Well, yeah, but we're unionized." Okay? So, and maybe this guy was right, okay, at one of our investor at the time. But now, that's what we're doing, is we're beefing up with people from outside this UPS world, UPS Freight world, okay, that we got, because we've tried. We've tried, but it's like, you know, you're trying to change a guy that's been in an environment for some 20-some years, and he's been used to not care too much about service, not care too much about cost, because it's just the way it is. You're trying to change this guy, but nah, it doesn't work, right? So, new broom sweeps clean. So, after three years of trying and trying and trying, okay, we said, "We got to change the recipe." Okay? And that's what we're doing now, okay? We're changing the recipe. So, we're going to bring more executives from some of our peers that's got experience in our world to turn this ship around and to change this mentality of, "We don't really care," right? And it's simple. Why we have executives that don't care or employees that don't care in that world is because the previous owner did not care about UPS Freight. I mean, they did not invest in the fleet, they did not invest in real estate, they did not invest in the technology, because for them, it was like, "Forget about it. I mean, we don't need that. Our focus is the other company, and we're doing great there." Okay, fine. So, all this, we tried to change this whole executive team there and improve them by giving them financial tools, better technology, better assets, et cetera, et cetera. But it is not working. I mean, if you look at the results, it is not working, right? So, we said, "Now, okay, guys, this does not work, okay?" So, we need now to change course, and that is what we are doing. Now, your first question was.
David Saperstein: Yeah, on logistics. What was that, Jordan? Could you repeat it?
Jordan Alliger: Yeah, just what is driving the logistics opposite brokerage.
Alain Bédard: Ah, yes.
Jordan Alliger: Last mile, you have other things in there.
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
David Saperstein: Yeah.
Alain Bédard: Yeah. So, on the logistics side, for sure. I mean, we're piggybacking on the OEM, right? So, the OEM, like PACCAR and DTNA, those guys are doing good. Well, for sure, we're going to do better, right? So, this is something that's helping us. The other thing also that's helped us is the acquisition we did, December of 2025, late last year, of two entrepreneurs that built a fabulous company. Okay? So now, with these guys, we are now involved into data center. We're involved also with one of our customers on the storage, the battery storage that these guys are building. I mean, those guys are really building a fantastic business. So, that's helping our logistics. Our U.S. last mile also is doing quite well. On the Canadian side, we've lost a little bit of business. We had a business with the banks in Canada, through Symcor, that was doing great. I mean, 15 years ago, that business was supposed to disappear, and now it's disappearing, right? So, we rode the horse until it dies, but that horse is dying on us right now. Okay. That's on the Canadian last mile operation. So, we have all kinds of puts and takes, but at the same time, we are growing the business organically in our logistics sector, piggybacking on, yes, we're big with two major OEMs, but we're also growing with the smaller guys, like the Hino and the Isuzu and all these guys. And for sure, I mean, on the EV side of the truck, that's something new for us. Okay. For sure, these guys will not use only one carrier. They will probably use three carriers. We'll be one of them. David Saperstein: Yeah, and the logistics, as you can tell, I mean, the margins are really top of the.
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
David Saperstein: The peer group, and growing fast, right? We did $49 million of operating income in the quarter. That is up from $31 million last year. And so, it is really a collection of asset-light businesses. This is not just commoditized brokerage at all. It is a collection of asset-light businesses where we have got really good market share, good barriers to entry, good connectivity with our customers.
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
David Saperstein: They are all, it is just a collection of great businesses that continues to grow.
Jordan Alliger: Thank you.
Operator: Your next question comes from Cameron Doerksen from National Bank. Please go ahead.
Cameron Doerksen: Yeah, thanks. Good morning. You touched a little bit on this already, but I'll maybe ask it again or a little different way. Just on the, I guess, the U.S. LTL business. I mean, obviously, this is a source of frustration for you and for investors as well.
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
Cameron Doerksen: But, if the desire, I guess, for the company as a whole is to become more asset-light, and obviously, you indicated that you're looking at potentially asset-light LTL acquisitions in the U.S. I mean, is there an option, or does it make sense at all to maybe divest the TForce Freight business in the U.S.? Alain Bédard: You know what, Cameron? We sold a few businesses in my 30 years life with TFI. We sold the waste to GFL, and we sold, what did we sell? Okay, the waste and CFI. So, the waste, the reason we sold the waste is because we couldn't grow it, right? Because we were trading at 6x and the market for waste was 10x, so we sold it. So, I mean, we're going to keep fighting, and I think that Kal's approach is, we're going to change the recipe. We're gonna change, I mean, we've invested tons of dollars with the asset, the fleet, and the real estate, the tools, et cetera, et cetera, and it's not working. So then, what's left? But we want those guys to be efficient, to be productive, and after improving everything except the human side of the business, and it's not working, well, then say, "Hey, guys, the problem is the human." I mean, there's no more excuse on the fleet. There's no more excuse on the financial tools or whatever. It's just that we have the wrong guys.
Cameron Doerksen: Okay. No, that's helpful. I'll leave it at one question. Thanks very much.
Alain Bédard: Okay.
Operator: Your next question comes from Kevin Chiang from CIBC. Please go ahead.
Kevin Chiang: Hey, thanks for taking my question here. Maybe if I just take a step back and I think back to the last cycle, and I know different factors were at play, but you achieved over $8 of EPS, clearly during a more robust volume environment. I think expectations were that you could reach a higher high as U.S. LTL hit the KPIs you wanted. But let's say excluding a recovery in U.S. LTL, is that level of EPS growth, like $8, $9, still achievable for the rest of the business, just given, clearly, TForce Freight wouldn't have been much of a contributor back four or five years ago?
Alain Bédard: Well, Kevin, I mean, I think that today, based on what I know about this market, that is still in, we're still in a freight recession, right? So, let's say that we accomplish the $1.40 in Q4. We end up the year at, what, $5.50 or something like that, okay, which is still far from $8. I mean, this is a long way from $8. Now, with all the tweaks that we have to do with the rest of our business, logistics and truckload and all that, can we add a buck, okay, in this freight environment? Maybe, okay? I've not seen 2027 plan yet, okay? I'm going to be in Toronto in two weeks to review all that with the team there. But it's difficult, until we have freight coming back to normal, okay? And we need the contribution of TForce Freight to be an $8 guy. If those guys continue to be minimal contribution to us, it's going to be tough for us to be back to $8. We need those guys to get the job done, right, to get to that $8. Now, don't forget, when we got $8.22, we didn't have JHT. We didn't have Daseke, okay? But don't forget also that we pay in terms of interest, because our debt is still around $2.2 billion, okay? We don't do anything of size, okay, in 2027. Our debt from $2.2 billion is going to go down to maybe, I don't know, down, let's say $500 million, okay? At 5%, okay, of interest cost, it's $25 million. After tax, let's say it's $20 million on 80 million shares. Okay, well, what is that? $0.25? Okay. So, we're heading in the right direction if this happens, but we're not at $8 at all, right? So, we need the freight market to come back to be an $8 guy, in my mind. And the contribution also of TForce Freight.
Kevin Chiang: That's helpful. You need the contribution. Maybe just a quick follow-up, just given where the stock is now, just changes in maybe near-term capital allocation. Do you lean more on the buyback here? You were active in October. Does that accelerate here, just given the move in your share price?
Alain Bédard: Well, for sure, I mean, Kevin, like you said, we bought back about 400,000 shares in October. We're at a crossroad right now, okay, based on what do you do? Do you do M&A, okay, or do you just buy back your stock and wait, let's say, six months, 12 months, to have more confirmation that this freight environment is changing? Or you just do some small tuck-ins, like we always do. So, I mean, this is, for us, it's going to be a major decision into 2027, is that based on the stock price, based on what's going on with our industry, if you just go back to, let's say, six months ago, and today, our stock is down, what, 30%, David, or about?
David Saperstein: Yeah.
Alain Bédard: Right? So, were we overvalued then, and now we're undervalued? But it's not just us. I mean, the industry in general is down big time, okay? So, it's going to be a balance that we're going to have to look at. So, for sure, we'll look at the reaction on the stock. We'll look at the reaction of our investors, okay, and what they're saying. And for us, if we don't do anything of size to buy back 1 million shares at $100, I don't know if the stock is $100, but we'll see, it's just $100 million. And we're going to generate probably, without any large M&A transaction, another $700 million-$800 million of cash in 2027, even if this soft environment continues. So, why take the risk of huge M&A when you got a stock that is in the doldrum?
David Saperstein: That's always been the beauty, right? That's why we have a 30-year track record of compounding so tremendously, is just that we generate so much free cash, and we reinvest it.
Alain Bédard: Right.
David Saperstein: We give back a solid amount to the shareholders in the form of a dividend, which has a very long track record of increasing each year. But the rest is reinvested, and it compounds over time. So, that has always been the key to the long-term success.
Alain Bédard: Yeah, absolutely.
Kevin Chiang: I appreciate you taking my question, and best of luck as you close out 2026 here.
Alain Bédard: Thank you.
Operator: Your next question comes from Bruce Chan from Stifel. Please go ahead.
Bruce Chan: Hey, good morning, gents. Just a couple of cleanups here. On the truckload side, you've made some nice progress on pricing, and I know you said, Alain, that you see some upside in bid season for next year. Just want to get a sense maybe for what you're seeing in terms of contract renewals. And then, David, is there anything that we should be thinking about as far as headwinds for driver cost inflation, given the tightness in the market?
Alain Bédard: Yeah. So, we know that contract rates, I mean, the guys are working on that. I mean, we have a customer, okay? Contract is due November 1st, and we've honored the contract, us. And we're saying, "Mr. Customer, you're going to have to pay 20% more." So, the guy says, "Ooh, this is a lot. I mean, can we extend the contract for another year?" And we said, "No. No, because this is reality." So, for sure, and also what we've done, what Steve has done is that now, we have a commercial team under one leader, which is Scott Hoppe, right? So, Scott sees everything that's going on, right? So, this customer, our friend Scott is involved, and for sure, this is what we need. Now, it's not easy when the market has to be adjusted 20% to reflect market condition. But, I mean, we've honored the contract. Now, this is reality, Mr. Customer. So, what we see in contract renewal is that prices are going up. Prices are going up. Now, to second leg of the question, like we said, we have pressure on labor costs. Why is that? Because everybody is looking for drivers. Right? And it's the eternal issue when, okay, you got more freight, although we don't have more freight, but we have less drivers availability. Well, everybody's looking for drivers right now, so that brings inflation, okay, to the salary, which, between you and me, I think is needed, okay, when you have a 3%, 4% inflation. So, you need to adjust the salary of those guys. And at the same time, we have to push customers around that this is the new reality, my friend, and this is the new price. And we're not in the business of practicing delivery just to have fun. No.
David Saperstein: Yeah. I think in terms of quantifying it, the revenue per truck per week, which we publish, is a really good indication of where pricing is, right? We're up 13%. That's where the facts really hit, right? Because it's one thing to get contract rate increases, but the question is how many miles do you get at those contract rates?
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
David Saperstein: It doesn't help you if a customer gives you a big rate increase and he doesn't give you any freight. So, where the rubber meets the road is really, what's the revenue per truck?
Alain Bédard: Yep.
David Saperstein: Is that going up or is it going down? In our case, it's going up 13%. So, that gives you a sense for realized pricing. Of course, there's a little bit of productivity, more miles in there. The beauty of our model is that in the face of driver shortage, difficulty recruiting, et cetera, we've been able to grow our revenue while decreasing our truck count. Why? Because we're brokering more. So, this enables us to sort of work through this driver inflation kind of situation more effectively, because we're actually reducing our driver pool.
Alain Bédard: Yeah.
David Saperstein: While increasing our revenue.
Bruce Chan: Okay, great. That's a helpful color. Then, just a last one here. Alain, you talked about LTL service levels. Any sense for directionally, where those are right now and where they're going?
Alain Bédard: Hey, you know what? We were heading in the right direction in 2025. I mean, from start of 2025, okay, everything, our service was improving big time. Then, we messed it up. We messed it up in 2026, right? Why is that? Well, first, we start the year with this issue with the weather. I mean, everybody's got issues with the weather, but it seems for us was more prevalent, okay. Then, we add volume, and, oh, the shit hit the fan, right? So, our service tanked. So, this is the wrong direction. Now, we've addressed that. So, from that disastrous nine months of 2026, now we're heading in the right direction in terms of, because we have stability now. We're at 19,000, 19,500, 20,000 shipments. Now we have stability, and now the focus is, guys, we have to deliver on time. We cannot lose customers' freight, okay, et cetera, et cetera. So, to improve the service, because that's the key. This is like the chicken and the egg. What comes first? Well, what comes first is the service, okay? Once you have the service, then you could be in a top-class carrier, and you can ask for more money. But until such time that you're a dog in terms of service, it's difficult to get the premium revenue per shipment, right? So, this is why the trend has to be, "Hey, guys, okay, forget about the first nine months of 2026. We shit the bed. Okay. But now, let's roll up our sleeve and do the job." This is what the team and the executive team that we're building, okay, gets.
Bruce Chan: Okay, great. Appreciate it.
